preprints.title: Light-dependent activation of TCP4 by the GATA25 transcription factor promotes petiole and hypocotyl elongation in Arabidopsis thaliana
preprints.abstract: Plants coordinate cell elongation with the daily light/dark cycle, an important adaptive strategy for optimizing growth under changing environmental conditions. However, the transcriptional mechanisms linking light signals to plant developmental growth remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified the GATA25 transcription factor as a regulator of petiole and hypocotyl elongation in response to light and photoperiod. Overexpression of GATA25 in Arabidopsis thaliana increased petiole and hypocotyl lengths and elevated TCP4 transcript levels. We demonstrated that GATA25 directly binds to the promoter of TCP4 and activates its transcription using transcriptional activation analysis, a glucocorticoid receptor-based inducible system, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and electrophoretic mobility shift assays. Furthermore, yeast two-hybrid assay and bimolecular fluorescence complementation analyses showed that GATA25 physically interacts with the E3 ubiquitin ligase COP1. Notably, overexpression of GATA25 did not increase TCP4 transcript levels in dark conditions, suggesting that GATA25 activity is suppressed in dark conditions. Based on these findings, we propose a model in which GATA25 is destabilized by COP1 in dark conditions, restricting TCP4 activation to the light conditions. Taken together, these findings provide a framework for understanding how the daily light/dark cycle regulates cell elongation in a photoperiod-dependent manner through the GATA25-TCP4 module.

last_author.name: Kim, W.-C.
last_author.affiliation: Kyungpook National University

preprints.title: Local and distal signals drive cell-type-specific leaf responses during shade avoidance
preprints.abstract: Plants reposition and grow their leaves towards optimal light conditions in a canopy. To achieve both horizontal and vertical displacement, plants need to simultaneously elongate their cells unidirectionally and maintain an elongation rate differential between the abaxial and adaxial side of the organ to bend. Exposure to Far-Red (FR) light enrichment can induce both responses, depending on where FR is sensed. Here we studied how plants maintain both growth responses simultaneously within the same organ. To deduce the regulatory mechanisms governing the simultaneous regulation of differential and unidirectional elongation, we performed both organ specific and single cell RNA sequencing experiments on plants exposed to local or whole plant FR enrichment. Single cell transcriptomics resolved that FR light signalling occurs through all cell types, but core components of the shade avoidance pathway are expressed cell type-specifically and require signalling across tissues to control growth plasticity. The upstream photoreceptor targets, including auxin biosynthesis-associated genes, in the leaf lamina are expressed in the epidermis, whilst auxin response gene expression in the petiole occurs also in the deeper tissues layers. We thus identified the remotely triggered differential growth transcriptome acting in the abaxial cortex and show that this is complemented by locally induced second transcriptome signature that is associated with unidirectional petiole elongation. The latter is induced across all cell types. We propose that this spatial distinction of transcriptional regulation of gene clusters could represent how differential and unidirectional growth can occur simultaneously in the same organ under FR light enrichment.

last_author.name: Pierik, R.
last_author.affiliation: Wageningen University and Research

preprints.title: Model-guided design of single-cargo, dual-attractor gene circuits
preprints.abstract: Dual-attractor gene networks program distinct states, guiding native cellular decision-making processes such as differentiation. Synthetic dual-attractor circuits (DACs) emulate native gene networks, directing cells to two different states starting from a single, genetically uniform population. However, existing DAC designs for mammalian cells often require multiple genetic cargoes, limiting their application to control cell fate in therapeutically relevant contexts. Here, we leverage model-guided tuning of compact biochemical and biophysical layers of regulation to program two cellular states using a single-cargo DAC. Through activator selection and layering microRNA-mediated mutual repression, we identify and resolve an imbalance between modules that biases states, allowing us to achieve balanced adoption of both states without relying on copy-number variation. Consolidating this optimized DAC into a single cargo, we use gene syntax to minimize bias, generating two balanced states from a single cargo of less than 11 kilobases. Overall, this work establishes design rules for combined biochemical and biophysical tuning of DACs to generate balanced cell states from a single-cargo design, paving the way for programming divergent cell-state trajectories and dual-fate systems.

last_author.name: Galloway, K. E.
last_author.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology

preprints.title: Pharmacologic inhibition of OLIG2 by CT-179 disrupts mitotic progression and enhances standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy in glioblastoma
preprints.abstract: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains uniformly fatal. The basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor OLIG2 is universally expressed in diffuse glioma, sustains the tumor-propagating stem-like fraction, and opposes p53-mediated genotoxic responses, but has historically been considered undruggable. We characterized CT-179, a brain-penetrant small-molecule OLIG2 inhibitor, as a candidate therapeutic for GBM. Methods: Target engagement was assessed by cellular thermal shift assay, differential scanning fluorimetry, crosslinking, and electrophoretic mobility shift assay. Anti-tumor activity was evaluated across eleven patient-derived GBM cell lines, in zebrafish oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-derived tumors, and orthotopic and subcutaneous GBM models, including combinations with radiotherapy plus temozolomide and with selective Bcl-2 family inhibitors. Results: CT-179 engaged OLIG2 and altered the conformation of dimerized OLIG2 on chromatin without preventing dimerization or fully displacing OLIG2 from DNA. CT-179 reduced OLIG2-positive OPCs and OPC-derived tumors in zebrafish and inhibited proliferation across all eleven GBM lines (IC50 < 360 nM), depleting the stem-like fraction and inducing apoptosis through mitotic catastrophe, mitotic slippage, or a hybrid response. RNA-seq across three patient-derived glioma stem cell lines identified {beta}-tubulin gene isoforms as the most strongly CT-179-down-regulated transcripts at the early time point and showed correlated {beta}-tubulin and OLIG2 expression in TCGA glioblastoma specimens. Combination with the Mcl-1 inhibitor S63845 or the Bcl-2/Bcl-xL/Bcl-w inhibitor ABT-737 produced greater-than-additive cytotoxicity. Oral CT-179 crossed the blood-brain barrier and extended median survival as a single agent across two independent adult orthotopic patient-derived backgrounds (GBM8 and G06); intraperitoneal CT-179 was associated with reduced intratumoral OLIG2 and Ki-67 staining in GBM8 orthotopic xenografts. Combination of CT-179 with radiotherapy and temozolomide eliminated all GBM8 and 7 of 8 GBM4 subcutaneous xenografts without weight loss and significantly extended survival when combined with radiotherapy in MGMT-unmethylated GBM6 orthotopic xenografts (CT-179 administered intraperitoneally). Conclusions: CT-179 is a brain-penetrant inhibitor of an established GBM driver with single-agent and combination activity across several orthotopic models, supporting clinical development for GBM and translational evaluation in other OLIG2-dependent CNS malignancies.

last_author.name: Johns, T. G.
last_author.affiliation: Monash University

preprints.title: Polyglutamine-expanded TBP rewires neuronal and muscle proteomes beyond transcription in a Drosophila model of SCA17
preprints.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 17 (SCA17) is an age-related neurodegenerative disorder caused by polyglutamine expansion in the TATA-binding protein (TBP). TBP is a core transcription factor, but pathogenic polyglutamine expansion likely rewires cellular programs beyond transcription. Here, we utilized Drosophila strains that express wild-type (WT) or pathogenic (SCA17) TBP in neurons or skeletal muscle, which we analyzed vs. controls via TMT mass spectrometry, profiling of eight post-translational modifications, and RNA-seq. Shared TBP-WT and TBP-SCA17 responses predominated, impacting ribosomes and mitochondria while repressing innate immunity. Disease-specific effects were narrower and tissue-dependent: SCA17 activated xenobiotic, retinoid, and glutathione-redox pathways in the CNS, but attenuated anabolism in muscle compared to TBP-WT. Many proteomic changes occurred independently of mRNA changes, implicating post-transcriptional mechanisms. Knockdown of select SCA17-regulated proteins reduced cytotoxicity, validating omics-identified modifiers of SCA17 pathology. These findings distinguish shared TBP dosage effects from disease-linked, tissue-specific polyglutamine responses and identify evolutionarily conserved targets for SCA17.

last_author.name: Todi, S. V.
last_author.affiliation: WAYNE STATE UNIVERSITY

preprints.title: SCN1A haploinsufficiency disrupts neural progenitor networks and accelerates neurogenesis in human Dravet syndrome forebrain assembloids
preprints.abstract: Dravet syndrome is a severe childhood neurological disorder caused mostly due to mutations in the sodium channel gene SCN1A. Although the disorder is widely attributed to dysfunction of inhibitory neurons, growing evidence suggests that disease mechanisms may begin much earlier during brain development. To investigate the developmental consequences of SCN1A haploinsufficiency, we generated patient-derived dorsal-ventral forebrain assembloids that model key features of human corticogenesis. We found that SCN1A was expressed in ventricular zone neural progenitors and that its reduced expression was associated with impaired growth, disrupted ventricular zone organization, and progressive depletion of progenitor populations. We further demonstrated reduced progenitor proliferation and self-renewal, accelerated cell-cycle exit, and premature neuronal differentiation, leading to increased production of excitatory neurons and enhanced network excitability. Single cell transcriptomic analyses revealed reduced cycling radial glial cells, accelerated progenitor maturation, and dysregulation of gap junction and calcium signaling pathways. Following these findings, we examined progenitor calcium activity and found that SCN1A haploinsufficiency disrupted coordinated functional network organization, resulting in reduced recurrent connectivity and fragmentation of functional cellular assemblies. These abnormalities occurred despite preserved intrinsic electrophysiological properties of individual progenitors, indicating a defect in population-level coordination rather than single cell electrophysiology. Together, our findings identify disrupted progenitor communication as an early developmental consequence of SCN1A haploinsufficiency and suggest that abnormalities within neural progenitor populations contribute to altered corticogenesis, excitatory neurogenesis, and circuit hyperexcitability in Dravet syndrome. This work expands current disease models beyond interneuron dysfunction and highlights the developing ventricular zone as a potential therapeutic target.

last_author.name: Kurrasch, D. M.
last_author.affiliation: University of Calgary

preprints.title: Self-extending DNA recording with stochastic and programmed writing
preprints.abstract: Recording cellular histories requires continued information accumulation while retaining earlier records. Infinite Printer couples DNA self-extension to regeneration of a writable terminal context. A single self-targeting prime-editing guide directs repeat extension, while base editing diversifies the accessible sequence in situ. A separate configuration uses auxiliary guides for specified payload writing. After three rounds of payload input, 4,436 distinct complete records contained identities from all three pools. Extended AC/AT records retained shared upstream marks, and complete-sequence readout distinguished endpoints sharing initial prefixes. Joint single-cell readout recovered 1,549 records and 7,669 combinations across 12,302 transcriptome-linked cell labels; spatial readout linked records to 11,330 capture spots. These results establish a resource for self-extending stochastic and programmed DNA recording with joint cellular and tissue readout, providing a foundation for future lineage applications.

last_author.name: Chen, D.
last_author.affiliation: Center for Translational Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou 510080, China

preprints.corresponding_institution: The First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University

preprints.title: Shoot to root transport of the HY5 transcription factor drives root developmental plasticity under neighbour shade.
preprints.abstract: Plants perceive competitors through the reflection of Far-Red light from neighbouring leaves. A decrease in the Red: Far-red light ratio (R:FR) is perceived by phytochrome photoreceptors and triggers elongation responses aboveground, allowing plants to anticipate future competition for light; their primary energy source. However, low R:FR perception by the shoot also prompts an alteration of root development, possibly to conserve resources. An important regulator of this response is the bZIP transcription factor ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 5 (HY5), which can be transported from the shoot to the root, where it suppresses auxin signaling and lateral root outgrowth. However, it remains unknown whether HY5 transport is the direct link between shoot-perceived low R:FR and a decrease in lateral root outgrowth. We therefore sought to uncover the mechanics and speed of HY5 transport. To this end, we constructed shoot-specific inducible lines to perform live-imaging of HY5 transport using a vertical confocal microscope. This allowed us to follow the transport and unloading of HY5 from the phloem into the protophloem pericycle, where it becomes nuclearly localized, in real time over a 24-hour period. To mimic plant competition, we applied supplemental FR light and observed that this increased the HY5 protein levels in the shoot and subsequent HY5 protein transport from shoot-to-root. Finally, we were able to show that shoot-expressed HY5 is necessary and sufficient to induce the root response to shoot perceived Far-Red light. This work showcases in detail how a small general transcription factor functions as a long-distance signal between shoot and root and integrates environmental signalling over long distances in the plant.

last_author.name: van Gelderen, K.
last_author.affiliation: Heidelberg University - Centre for Organismal Studies

preprints.corresponding_institution: Heidelberg University - Centre for Organismal Studies

preprints.title: Spatial transcriptomics maps region and isoform specific brain alterations in mdx and mdx4cv models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy
preprints.abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is accompanied by cognitive and neurodevelopmental difficulties. To investigate how the loss of different dystrophin isoforms affects gene expression across brain regions, we performed spatial transcriptomics on brains from mdx and mdx4cv mouse models (lacking Dp427 or Dp427+Dp140 respectively) and healthy controls aged 2 weeks. Both dystrophic models showed transcriptional changes converging on myelin and oligodendrocyte biology and oxidative phosphorylation, but with distinct regional patterns. In mdx mice, myelin genes were upregulated in the amygdala and hippocampus and downregulated in fiber tract regions, while mitochondrial genes were upregulated in most regions but downregulated in the thalamus and isocortex. In mdx4cv mice, myelin genes were broadly upregulated and mitochondrial genes downregulated across almost all regions. Direct comparison between mdx and mdx4cv mice demonstrated that the additional loss of Dp140 expanded localized myelin upregulation across the brain and shifts the mitochondrial response toward widespread downregulation. These differences in regional changes between the mouse models is in line with their dystrophin isoform(s) loss. Our findings provide a molecular basis for the brain-related impairments of DMD and a foundation for future therapeutic studies.

last_author.name: Mahfouz, A.
last_author.affiliation: Leiden University Medical Center

preprints.title: Synchronised developmental partitioning of visual opsins across parental subgenomes in allopolyploid Barbus barbus
preprints.abstract: Hybridisation and whole-genome duplication generate evolutionary novelty by combining and duplicating divergent parental genomes. Yet, how organisms differentially deploy duplicated gene repertoires across development remains poorly understood. The vertebrate visual system provides an excellent model for addressing this question because colour vision depends on the tightly regulated expression of opsin genes, which often undergo pronounced ontogenetic changes. Here, using comparative transcriptomics, we show that the allopolyploid common barbel (Barbus barbus) has evolved coordinated developmental partitioning of duplicated cone opsin genes. During ontogeny, the short-wavelength-sensitive opsins SWS1 and SWS2 switch expression between parental-subgenome ohnologs, while the middle-wavelength-sensitive RH2 switches between tandem paralogs, with all three transitions being synchronised. In contrast, the long-wavelength-sensitive LWS ohnologs from both parental genomes remain co-expressed throughout development. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing further revealed a strongly rod-dominated retina and largely conserved expression of phototransduction genes across recent ohnologs. The retention of all 14 visual opsin genes and their differential developmental deployment in common barbel highlights the value of independently evolved allopolyploid lineages for investigating the evolutionary consequences of genome duplication. More broadly, our findings show how hybridisation and genome duplication can enable divergent expression of parental gene copies, potentially contributing to sensory adaptation over evolutionary timescales.

preprints.title: The development of coarse and fine feature tuning in infant visual cortex
preprints.abstract: Objects can be recognized from visual features at multiple spatial scales, from coarse global shape to fine local detail. How infant visual cortex encodes these features across the visual hierarchy, however, remains unknown. We combined awake infant fMRI with developmentally inspired deep neural networks (DNNs) trained and tested with different levels of image blur to probe cortical tuning to coarse and fine visual features. V1 showed mature tuning to coarse and fine features by 2 months. In contrast, infant extrastriate cortex (V2-V4) followed a protracted developmental trajectory and was biased toward coarse object features relative to adults. This relative bias persisted at 9 months and was not readily explained by developing acuity. The sustained coarse-feature bias contrasted with DNNs, in which low-spatial-frequency representations took longest to converge with visual cortex during training, revealing distinct developmental biases in object-feature tuning in biological and artificial visual systems.

last_author.name: Cusack, R.
last_author.affiliation: Trinity College Institute of Neuroscience, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland

preprints.title: The interferon-gamma response pathway is a targetable driver of FSHD muscular dystrophy progression
preprints.abstract: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is a leading neuromuscular disorder caused by the aberrant expression of the transcription factor double homeobox 4 (DUX4) in skeletal muscle. While DUX4 is normally restricted to early embryonic development, its reactivation in FSHD triggers chronic inflammation and progressive muscle degeneration. However, the precise molecular links between DUX4 and persistent immune activation remain poorly understood. Here, we show that DUX4 induces a viral mimicry-like pathway that is fundamentally uncoupled from canonical type I interferon (IFN) activation. Instead, DUX4 establishes a non-canonical innate immune state dominated by IFN-gamma signaling, providing a mechanistic explanation for the non-resolving inflammation characteristic of the disease. We demonstrate that while IFN-gamma treatment alone is sufficient to recapitulate key DUX4 pathogenic effects, its inhibition rescues muscle inflammation and halts disease progression in FSHD models. These findings define a skewed viral mimicry process driven by a disease-specific transcription factor and identify IFN-gamma as a primary therapeutic target for tissue-informed immunomodulation in muscular dystrophy.

last_author.name: Gabellini, D.
last_author.affiliation: Gene Expression Regulation Unit, Division of Genetics and Cell Biology, IRCCS Ospedale San Raffaele, Milan, Italy

preprints.corresponding_institution: Gene Expression Regulation Unit, Division of Genetics and Cell Biology, IRCCS Ospedale San Raffaele, Milan, Italy

preprints.title: U-Chrom: a unified framework for single-cell and spatial 3D genome data
preprints.abstract: Single-cell Hi-C, spatial Hi-C and chromatin tracing measure the same genomes in incompatible formats. ChromData, one data model, indexes all three by cell and genomic bin; an open-source toolkit, linked browser and 22-dataset atlas build on it. Applied to ten mouse brain datasets of all three assays, the same calls rank cell types alike by short- over long-range proximity, and contact-based reconstructions largely place cell-type differences where imaging does.

last_author.name: Xu, W.
last_author.affiliation: Stanford University

preprints.title: XplainTDA: Explaining the topological structure of single-cell multi-omics data through perturbation
preprints.abstract: Single-cell experiments have improved our ability to study biological systems by profiling thousands of cells simultaneously. The data can be viewed as a point cloud in a proper experimental space, whose shape is defined by the gene regulatory network. Persistent homology has been proposed as a method for studying the intrinsic structure of data and has shown the potential to reveal novel insights. Existing approaches focus on detecting topological features or groups of cells, without a focus on explainability and interpretability. Here, we introduce an explainable topological data analysis framework for single-cell data (XplainTDA) that identifies molecular determinants underlying the topological structure of the data via a perturbation-based approach. Across omics and data sets, we show that the method is stable, reproducible, and interpretable, extending persistent homology from topological description to molecular interpretation.
preprints.corresponding_institution: Institute of Computational Biology, Computational Health Center, Helmholtz Munich, Munich, Germany

preprints.title: hvantk: an agentic multi-omics framework for variant annotation and analysis
preprints.abstract: Large-scale genetic variant analysis involves multiple computational steps, data formats, gene and variant annotation sources and compute requirements. Some of the steps like joint calling for large cohorts are run on large compute clusters, while gene/variant classification algorithms can be run in a desktop computer. At the same time, variant annotations such as gene expression and gene constraints metrics from gnomAD are provided in different formats, by resources that frequently change their versions. Here, we present hvantk, a framework that provides a common data model for large-scale annotation and analysis of genetic variants, by extending popular data formats such as Hail MatrixTable and AnnData. hvantk agentically integrates 21 public multi-omic data providers as plugins that a developer, bioinformatician or an AI agent can author without modifying the framework's core, drives analysis workflows using agent skills, and scales from single desktop computers to high-performance computing clusters. We used hvantk for reanalysing three case-control cohorts, comprising congenital heart disease (CHD), developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Epi25) and schizophrenia (SCHEMA). Re-ranking of gene-based burden testing results using multi-omic annotations improved the recovery of curated disease genes from 26% to 49% in CHD, 40% to 48% in Epi25 and 51% to 54% in SCHEMA, among the top decile re-ranked genes. Expression at bulk and single-cell levels were the features contributing the most over a baseline of burden, gene constraint and publication count.
preprints.corresponding_institution: Institute of Medical Genetics, University Medicine Oldenburg, Carl von Ossietzky University, Oldenburg, Germany

preprints.title: Functional dissection of ultraconserved non-coding regions present near the Hoxd complex in vertebrates
preprints.abstract: Ultraconserved non-coding elements (UCEs) exhibit near-perfect sequence conservation across vertebrate genomes, implying severe evolutionary constraint and essential biological functions. Near the vertebrate Hoxd complex, a master regulator of axial patterning and limb morphogenesis, three Conserved Regions (CR1, CR2, and CR3), each longer than 200 bp, show exceptional sequence conservation and drive robust regulatory activity in transient reporter assays. To investigate their endogenous in vivo functions, we used CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to generate a series of deletions of varying sizes spanning CR2 and CR3, individually and in combination, within hoxd complex in zebrafish. Screening thousands of founder embryos revealed a clear size and conservation-dependent relationship between deletion extent and viability: complete deletion of core CR2, CR3, or the combined CR2/3 loci could not be transmitted through the germline, whereas the smaller and least-conserved deletion, a 626-bp subregion of CR2, was the only allele to yield a stable, homozygous-viable line. Our results indicate that the core ultraconserved sequences are developmentally indispensable, whereas flanking, less conserved sequences can be removed without consequence. Detailed phenotypic and molecular characterization of the mutant embryos revealed normal primary and secondary body axis formation, intact somite segmentation, and unperturbed craniofacial and pectoral fin development. Expression of hoxd complex genes showed no significant change in mutant embryos by RNA-ISH or RT-qPCR, although RT-qPCR revealed a consistent, modest upward trend at 24 and 48 hpf, raising the possibility that the deleted subregion normally contributes a weak repression of overall hoxd complex genes transcription. While this study reveals some functional aspects of ultraconserved elements, much more remains to be uncovered.

last_author.name: Mishra, R. K.
last_author.affiliation: CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CSIR-CCMB), Habsiguda, Uppal Road, Hyderabad, Telangana, 500007, India

preprints.corresponding_institution: Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology

preprints.title: Genomic foundation models do not yet boost common variant discovery beyond standard functional annotations
preprints.abstract: Genomic foundation models (GFMs) use large-scale AI to model genetic sequences and their influence on molecular phenotypes. While GFMs have shown promise in rare variant analysis, their utility for common variant discovery remains untested. Using the surrogate functional false discovery rate framework for functionally informed GWAS discovery, we compared standard functional annotations (baselineLD) with annotations derived from three leading GFMs: the sequence-to-function models AlphaGenome and Borzoi, and the genomic language model GPN-Star. Across 27 UK Biobank traits, GPN-Star decreased locus discovery relative to a standard GWAS, whereas AlphaGenome and Borzoi increased discovery but by less than baselineLD (medians 1.8%, 3.8%, and 5.1%). When we combined the GFM and baselineLD annotations, there was no increase over baselineLD alone (median changes -0.1% to 0.2%), suggesting that AlphaGenome and Borzoi mostly capture information already in baselineLD. Thus, GFMs may require larger corpora or trait-specific feature engineering to improve discovery beyond standard functional annotations.

preprints.title: Survival-associated cellular communication networks in human solid cancers
preprints.abstract: Single-cell atlases have enabled the prediction of human cell-cell communication (CCC) networks in cancer, but whether predicted communication networks have clinical significance is not well understood. Here, we integrated a pan-solid cancer scRNA-seq atlas comprising 78 cell types from 318,426 quality-controlled cells with bulk RNA-seq and clinical outcome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to develop Single-cell-based Kaplan-Meier Analysis Network (SKyNet). SKyNet prioritizes ligand-receptor interactions associated with overall survival across 11 human solid cancers, predicting unique interactions not inferred by previous CCC algorithms. In pancreatic adenocarcinoma, SKyNet-predicted endothelial-pericyte interactions were associated with poor outcomes that were validated by independent spatial transcriptomics and survival cohorts. In lung adenocarcinoma, lymphatic endothelial cell interactions consisting of collagen-integrin pairs were associated with poorer survival outcomes. In kidney renal clear cell carcinoma and kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma, fibroblast communication networks displayed disparate survival associations, with the DSC2-DSG2 axis associated with better survival outcomes. Thus, SKyNet provides a hypothesis-generating framework for cell type-specific communication pathways associated with patient outcomes.

last_author.name: O'Sullivan, T.
last_author.affiliation: UCLA

preprints.title: APLNR regulates directed migration to spatially pattern mesoderm in human gastruloids
preprints.abstract: During human gastrulation, mesoderm progenitors migrate while acquiring distinct identities. Whether this movement contributes to subsequent patterning remains unclear. Here, we identify the apelin receptor (APLNR) as a regulator of directed migration of mesoderm in human gastruloids. TBXT+ cells ingress basally and disperse from the PS-like region toward epiblast-like cells. Tracking reveals that this dispersal reflects a directional bias rather than increased speed. APLNR is enriched in nascent mesoderm, while its ligand APELA is expressed in adjacent epithelial cells. Control gastruloids exhibit fourfold greater dispersal than APLNR-depleted gastruloids despite modest speed differences, consistent with a model of chemotaxis by an epithelial ligand field. Paraxial and lateral mesoderm differentiation competence is preserved following APLNR depletion, while signaling programs and central FOXC2+ paraxial organization are altered. These findings support a role for APLNR-dependent guidance in positioning competent mesoderm progenitors for subsequent patterning.

last_author.name: Gardel, M.
last_author.affiliation: University of Chicago

preprints.title: BiNVaST: niche boundary-preserving and synthetic data-guided variational autoencoders for concordant inference across high-resolution spatial transcriptomic platforms
preprints.abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables subcellular spatially resolved transcript profiling but remains difficult to annotate in complex tissues because of gene coverage and super sparseness in expression. These challenges are amplified in cancer research, where neoplastic cell states and rare immune cells in tumor microenvironment are often poorly captured by generic references and/or cell typing tools exclusively built on molecular profile. Here, we present BiNVaST, a niche boundary-preserving and dual-branch variational autoencoder fused with statistical simulator for reliable cell typing across multiple spatial platforms. It generates platform-adjusted in silico training data by integrating query spatial profile and user-defined pre-annotated single-cell reference through Singular Value Decomposition and Optimal Transport, combining molecular similarity and spatial proximity to predict segmented cell labels. BiNVaST was benchmarked against existing methods across Xenium, CosMx, Stereo-seq, Visium HD platforms using six specimens from four tissue types. This tool is sensitive in detecting divergent tumor cell states and improves the cross-platform concordance, distinguishing disease-specific neoplastic and non-neoplastic cellular subpopulations and supporting robust cellular or niche inferences in heterogeneous tissues.

last_author.name: Li, Q.
last_author.affiliation: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital

preprints.title: Heterochronic Uncoupling of Brain and Face Morphogenesis Drives Premature Fusion in Ciliary Transition Zone Mutants
preprints.abstract: Normal facial development is highly coordinated with embryonic brain expansion, suggesting the forebrain acts as a physical scaffold dictating the spatial timing of facial prominence apposition and fusion. To test this idea, we compared B9d1 ciliary transition zone mutants, which exhibit altered Hedgehog signaling and premature facial fusion, to a normal murine developmental morphospace. At e11.5, mutant brains are significantly reduced in size, yet intrinsic facial prominence size remains largely normal. Projecting e11.5 and e12.5 mutants into the normal morphospace reveals a severe heterochronic uncoupling: the delayed, narrowed neurocranium mechanically forces normal-sized facial prominences into premature convergence. These results indicate that when brain growth slows, facial prominences initiate contact earlier in restricted spatial bounds. Conversely, this model predicts that an accelerated, expanded brain may act as a physical wedge, increasing the likelihood of cleft lip. By mathematically modeling these structural dependencies, we propose that palatogenesis operates on a continuous phenotypic spectrum, where premature fusion and cleft lip represent alternative physical outcomes conditioned on the underlying brain developmental trajectory.

last_author.name: Young, N. M.
last_author.affiliation: University of California San Francisco

preprints.title: LineageFlow: Growth-Corrected State Dynamics for Probabilistic Cell-Fate Prediction
preprints.abstract: Single-cell lineage tracing links early transcriptional states to the fates of their descendants, but forecasting clonal fate remains challenging because differentiation and unequal cell expansion jointly shape descendant populations. Here we introduce LineageFlow, a computational framework that combines continuous-time cell-state transitions, relative net growth and state-conditioned generative flows to predict future fate distributions and transcriptional profiles from early single-cell measurements. In clone-disjoint evaluations of lineage-traced hematopoiesis, LineageFlow improves fate prediction and expression-distribution accuracy over matched computational baselines. A separately retrained analysis of cord-blood lineage data shows a similar advantage at a longer prediction horizon. Controlled simulations show that accounting for differential growth improves fate prediction when descendant states expand at different rates, while offering little benefit under equal growth. These findings highlight the importance of modeling state transitions and relative expansion together when predicting the fate of unseen clones.

last_author.name: Zhang, W.
last_author.affiliation: Tsinghua University

preprints.title: LiverHomo: An Integrated and Interactive Human Liver Single-Cell Atlas with Protein Interaction and Cell-Cell Communication Networks
preprints.abstract: LiverHomo is an integrated cell atlas developed from publicly available human liver single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets spanning healthy and diverse liver disease contexts. While several single-cell resources for the human liver are available, LiverHomo provides broad disease coverage and extends transcriptomic exploration through the integration of protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks and cell-cell interactions. LiverHomo provides an interactive web portal (https://liverhomo.org) for exploring cellular composition, gene expression, differentially expressed genes, Gene Ontology annotations, cell-cell interactions, and context-specific PPI networks across diseases and cell types. To facilitate intuitive access to these multidimensional data, the portal incorporates Ask LiverHomo, a natural-language assistant that interprets user queries and directs users to relevant analyses and visualizations. Interactive histograms, violin plots, network visualizations, and metadata exploration enable users to examine the atlas at cellular, transcriptomic, and protein-interaction levels, while the underlying data are readily accessible for further analysis. Together, LiverHomo provides an integrated and accessible resource for investigating cellular and molecular alterations across human liver health and disease.

last_author.name: Zhao, H.
last_author.affiliation: University of Texas Medical Branch

preprints.title: Odad1 is Required for Deployment of Axonemal Outer Arm Dyneins and Embryonic Left-Right Patterning
preprints.abstract: Motile cilia generate fluid flow required for development and tissue homeostasis. Defects in ciliary motility cause Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), presenting with situs inversus, infertility, chronic respiratory disease, and hydrocephalus. Ciliary beating requires outer dynein arms (ODAs), anchored to microtubules by the ODA docking complex (ODA-DC). ODAD1 is an ODA-DC component and a known PCD protein. ODAD1 alleles are often associated with human laterality defects, however Odad1 has not been reported to localize to 9+0 axonemes. Here, we show that GFP-Odad1 localizes to nodal cilia (9+0) in the gastrocoel roof plate (GRP), the frog's equivalent to the mammalian node where left-right asymmetry is first established. We found that Odad1 knockdown (KD) disrupts left-right patterning in Xenopus, with loss of pitx2 expression and abnormal gut looping reflecting defective 9+0 nodal cilia at the GRP. In 9+2 multiciliated cells (MCC) axonemes, Odad1 loss impaired deployment of ODA motors and ODA-DC subunits, disrupting ciliary motility. Two patient-derived truncating ODAD1 alleles were similarly unstable, failing to rescue ODA docking in MCCs or left-right patterning at the GRP. Together, these results show ODAD1 is required for ODA-DC assembly in both 9+0 and 9+2 cilia, linking its loss to ciliary motility and left-right patterning defects in ODAD1-associated ciliopathy.

last_author.name: Wallingford, J. B.
last_author.affiliation: University of Texas at Austin

preprints.title: Pan-cancer nucleosome landscapes reveal tumor heterogeneity and inform cell-free DNA-based detection
preprints.abstract: Background: Nucleosome positioning and occupancy are fundamental features of chromatin organization, yet their variation across human cancers and potential utility for noninvasive cancer detection remain poorly characterized. Methods: We systematically characterized nucleosome organization across 410 primary tumors spanning 23 cancer types using ATAC-seq, establishing a high-confidence pan-cancer nucleosome atlas validated by independent MNase-seq data. We characterized shared and cancer-type-enriched nucleosome patterns, investigated their associations with tumor heterogeneity and regulatory alterations, and evaluated tissue-derived nucleosome signatures for cancer classification and detection using circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA). Results: The atlas identified shared and cancer-type-enriched nucleosomes associated with distinct regulatory programs. Notably, nucleosome occupancy provided information complementary to chromatin accessibility for tumor stratification and revealed molecular heterogeneity within individual cancers, including subgroups associated with Basal-like breast cancer. In hepatocellular carcinoma, differential nucleosome analysis revealed cancer-associated chromatin remodeling involving regulatory pathways, transcription factor motifs, and candidate genes. Importantly, tissue-derived nucleosome signatures were detectable in cfDNA, enabling classification among three cancer types (AUROC = 0.877) and colorectal cancer detection (AUROC = 0.930), with an AUROC of 0.773 in an independent validation cohort. We also developed OncoNucAtlas, a publicly accessible database facilitating exploration of these nucleosome landscapes. Conclusions: Our study cancer-associated nucleosome organization as a complementary source of epigenomic information and demonstrates the potential of tissue-derived nucleosome signatures for cfDNA-based cancer detection. The pan-cancer atlas provides a resource for investigating tumor heterogeneity and developing noninvasive cancer detection approaches.

last_author.name: Li, Y.
last_author.affiliation: Soochow University

preprints.title: Patterned membrane recycling balances apical and lateral cell surfaces to confine tissue deformation under stretch
preprints.abstract: During development, epithelia undergo large stretches, but how tissues confine the resulting deformations and stresses to specific regions is poorly understood. Here, we show that during Drosophila dorsal closure, the epidermis confines deformation through a developmentally controlled, patterned increase in apical cell surface. Dorsal cells respond to stretch by expanding their apical surface and flattening, whereas ventral cells do not expand nor flatten, even when over-stretched and despite reorganizing their actomyosin. Both shape changes require Rab11-dependent membrane recycling, showing that cell height and apical area are actively controlled rather than passively set by stretch. The Dpp/Brinker pathway restricts this remodeling to the dorsal epidermis. A vertex model shows that localized remodeling is sufficient to pattern tissue deformation and to reduce stresses, including in the ventral, non-remodeling, region. Tissue deformation is thus spatially confined by developmental patterning of the balance between apical and lateral surfaces through membrane recycling, rather than by cytoskeletal forces.

last_author.name: Solon, J.
last_author.affiliation: Instituto Biofisika

preprints.title: The Hox code abolishes anatomical variation in an insect gonad
preprints.abstract: Phenotypic traits can vary based on genes or environment. Nevertheless, some quantitative traits remain invariant. Understanding the developmental mechanisms that generate such invariance can reveal how phenotypic robustness evolves. Insect reproductive capacity is largely determined by the number of gamete-producing subunits within the gonad, providing a tractable system to investigate these mechanisms as they operate on a quantitative trait that impacts fitness. In most insects, gonad subunit number varies within and between species. Here, we investigate gonad development in the milkweed bug Oncopeltus fasciatus, wherein subunit number is invariant. We show that subunit number is established during embryogenesis, when some abdominal segments, but not others, specify somatic gonad precursors. The position and number of these precursors depend on segment identity, and experimentally modified segment number or Hox-mediated segment identity changes the number of gonad subunits. Thus, O. fasciatus establishes invariant subunit number by coupling gonad development to segmental patterning machinery. We propose that co-option of the Hox code provides a developmental mechanism for generating robustness in gonad subunit number and may thereby contribute to the evolution of reproductive capacity in other insects.

last_author.name: Extavour, C. G.
last_author.affiliation: Harvard University & HHMI

preprints.title: X-SPEAR: An Extensible Framework for Spatial Panel Evaluation and Refinement
preprints.abstract: Targeted spatial transcriptomics platforms such as Xenium require a predefined gene panel, and the genes in that panel are detected less efficiently, and to gene-specific degrees, in the spatial assay than in the single-cell reference used to choose them. We present X-SPEAR, a framework that couples DART marker selection with probe-level off-target assessment. DART learns short, interpretable Boolean gene rules and assembles several gene-disjoint rules per cell type. Its detection-aware training thins the reference to per-gene detection rates measured in a different, already completed experiment, so no Xenium data from the target tissue are needed before the panel is ordered. On held-out Xenium data from ovarian cancer, mouse brain and cervical cancer, DART substantially outperformed existing marker-selection methods at matched panel size, by 0.04-0.11 macro-F1 over Wilcoxon rank-sum, 0.04-0.08 over COSG and 0.10-0.18 over NS-Forest, and it reached Wilcoxon's best accuracy with 42-69% fewer genes. Ablations show that most of this gain comes from detection-aware training, which also improves other rank-based selectors and requires a detection profile measured with the same assay chemistry. At similar accuracy, DART's rule structure adds rules that faithfully summarise the downstream classifier, robustness to single-probe loss across 45 retinal ganglion cell subtypes, and better resolution of closely related cell states. We are applying X-SPEAR to design a Xenium panel for mouse retinal ganglion cell subtypes, and its in situ evaluation is in progress. X-SPEAR is available as an open-source Python package.

last_author.name: Cheng, Y.
last_author.affiliation: Penn Medicine

preprints.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Assay-Aware Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction
preprints.abstract: Machine learning models for molecular discovery often train on bioactivity data from heterogeneous assays, yet assay context is rarely explicitly represented. We investigate whether natural-language assay descriptions provide predictive information beyond molecular and protein representations. We develop ACL-DTI (Assay-aware Contrastive Learning-based Drug Target Interaction) and MAMMAL-AsAP, an assay-context extension of MAMMAL-DTI. Across five triplet-disjoint random splits, assay-aware models achieve competitive or improved performance over assay-agnostic baselines. Among the evaluated models, MAMMAL-AsAP achieves the highest (R^2) of 0.7198 +/- 0.0085. Masking experiments show that ACL-DTI is robust to incomplete assay descriptions, exhibiting the smallest reductions in R^2 among the evaluated models when masking the target name, assay technique, or both: 0.0228 +/- 0.0064, 0.0406 +/- 0.0113, and 0.0620 +/- 0.0190, respectively. These results indicate that assay descriptions contain predictive information not fully captured by molecular structures and protein sequences, and reveal architecture-dependent differences in how this information is exploited.

last_author.name: Sethi, T.
last_author.affiliation: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology Delhi

preprints.corresponding_institution: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology Delhi

preprints.title: Contextual Biomedical Language Models for Imbalance-Aware Drug-Food Interaction Classification
preprints.abstract: Drug-food interactions (DFIs) are essential to patient safety because they can alter drug effectiveness or cause side effects. Automated classification of DFIs is difficult because of unstructured textual data, semantic ambiguity, and class imbalance, especially when separating neutral interactions. This paper presents an imbalance-aware deep learning approach for classifying drug-food interactions into three classes: safe, neutral, and unsafe. A structured dataset is created from textual drug interaction descriptions by extracting drug-food pairs and labeling them using rule-based heuristics. To address class imbalance, we apply class weighting and focal loss while fine-tuning the context-aware BioBERT language model. Our experiments show that the approach reaches an accuracy of 85% and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.77, with a notable improvement on the minority neutral class (F1-score of 0.56). The main novelty of this work is the combination of contextual biomedical language modeling with imbalance-aware deep learning, enabling more effective classification of DFI datasets.

preprints.title: EG-BINN: Parameter-Efficient Ensembling of Gated Biologically Informed Neural Networks for Epigenetic Age Estimation
preprints.abstract: Epigenetic aging clocks are widely used to evaluate biological aging, disease risk, and clinical interventions. However, most existing clocks rely on linear models that overlook nonlinear relationships between age and methylation patterns, or on deep learning architectures that are parameter-intensive and difficult to interpret. We developed EG-BINN, a parameter-efficient ensemble of biologically informed neural networks that uses sample-specific gating to modulate representations across biologically annotated nodes. Trained on 93 multi-tissue datasets, EG-BINN achieved the lowest mean and median absolute errors among matched linear and nonlinear baselines in five-fold cross-validation, as well as the lowest mean absolute and root mean squared errors across eight held-out Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets. Analysis of the gating mechanism revealed widespread associations between pathway gate values and age, including trajectories that varied across blood, adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and liver. Across 11 TCGA cohorts, EG-BINN identified significant tumor--normal differences in residual epigenetic age acceleration in six cohorts, whereas Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) highlighted recurrent pathway nodes contributing to tumor age predictions. EG-BINN combines accurate pan-tissue age prediction with an explainable architecture for examining biologically labeled nodes across age, tissue, and disease contexts.

preprints.title: Establishment of Rabbit Formative-like Pluripotent Cells by Bidirectional Modulation of WNT Signaling Pathway
preprints.abstract: The generation of embryonic stem cells (ESCs) with full developmental capacity and robust chimera-forming potential remains a major bottleneck for most non-rodent mammalian species including rabbits, an important animal both for biomedicine and agriculture. Formative pluripotency is a unique intermediate state bridging the naive and primed pluripotent states, which is defined by distinct molecular signatures, intrinsic competence for primordial germ cell (PGC) specification, and unique developmental adaptability to early embryonic microenvironments. Here, we established a novel culture medium termed KFiC, which could bidirectionally and coordinately modulate the WNT/{beta}-catenin signaling pathway via combined treatment of WNT activator CHIR99021 and inhibitor IWR-1. The KFiC culture system enables efficient derivation and stable long-term self-renewal of rbESCs with consistent formative-like pluripotent characteristics. KFiC-cultured rbESCs (KFiC-rbESCs) form compact, undifferentiated colonies, maintain intact genomic stability, and recapitulate the transcriptional landscape of pre-implantation epiblast cells, accompanied by sustained high expression of the core formative pluripotency marker OTX2. Functionally, KFiC-rbESCs possess efficient PGC differentiation competence and extensively contribute to embryonic development after microinjection into rabbit morulae, displaying their superior developmental plasticity. Notably, the KFiC system can stabilize an intermediate formative-like pluripotent state in mouse, human, and porcine pluripotent stem cells, and KFiC-adapted mouse ESCs retain potent chimera-forming ability. Collectively, this study establishes a reliable culture platform for generating and maintaining formative-like rbESCs. This cross-species compatible system provides a promising foundation for further optimizing naive-level pluripotency in rbESCs and facilitates the generation of genetically engineered rabbit disease models.

last_author.name: Lai, L.
last_author.affiliation: Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Stem Cell and Regenerative Medicine, Guangzhou Institutes of Biomedicine and Health, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

preprints.corresponding_institution: Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Stem Cell and Regenerative Medicine, Guangzhou Institutes of Biomedicine and Health, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

preprints.title: GOLDEN: Gene expression and allele-informed decomposition for genetic heterogeneity in spatial transcriptomic data
preprints.abstract: Motivation Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables exploration of cellular interactions, including immune responses. However, current methods rely on pathologists, with limitations in addressing genetic heterogeneity, where niches harboring nonclonal cells, including placental or allograft tissues, are present. Deciphering these interindividual mixtures remains challenging. Results For deciphering interindividual heterogeneity in ST, we developed GOLDEN (Gene expressiOn and aLlele-informed DEcomposition for geNetic heterogeneity), which involves an allele-aware multitask network that encodes spot-level expressions into shared latent representations. Incorporating allele features, dual heads classify spot identity (target, nontarget, or mixed) and estimate target fractions. We utilized synthetic ST data with spot-level ground truth using semiallogeneic single-cell profiles. For these synthetic benchmarks, GOLDEN achieved reliable deconvolution, with high correlation (Pearson's r = 0.977) and low error (mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.045) in fraction estimation and consistent predictions across real-world STs. These predictions were genetically validated. Using GOLDEN, resolving spot-level genetic heterogeneity is feasible. Availability and implementation GOLDEN and the simulation code for ST are available at https://github.com/othertics/GOLDEN.

last_author.name: Paik, H.
last_author.affiliation: KISTI

preprints.title: HyARQ: a Snakemake workflow for allele-specific read counting and quality control in F1 hybrids
preprints.abstract: Summary Allele-specific analysis in F1 hybrids allows direct assessment of how cis-regulatory variation contributes to differences in gene expression and other regulatory features. However, allele-specific analyses are sensitive to errors arising from multiple sources, including mapping bias and technical variation, requiring careful processing and quality control. These challenges are compounded by the fact that workflows for different molecular assays are often developed separately, making consistent analysis and quality control across assays difficult. Here, we introduce HyARQ, a Snakemake workflow for allele-specific read counting and quality control across RNA-seq, MOA-seq, ATAC-seq, and ChIP-seq data. HyARQ integrates assay-specific preprocessing, mapping to concatenated parental genomes, filtering, counting at paired parental genes or regulatory regions, and quality control within a common workflow. Using simulated datasets with known parental origin and allelic proportions, we show that HyARQ accurately recovers expected parental proportions with minimal cross-parent assignment across all four assay types. We further applied HyARQ to real RNA-seq, MOA-seq, ATAC-seq, and ChIP-seq datasets and generated paired parental counts and assay-specific quality control outputs for each assay. HyARQ provides a standardized and reproducible framework for allele-specific analysis across multiple molecular layers and facilitates downstream studies of cis-regulatory variation in F1 hybrids.

preprints.title: LigRNA: High-accuracy prediction of RNA-ligand binding sites via dynamic chemical complementarity and language model encoding
preprints.abstract: RNA-binding small molecules represent a validated therapeutic modality, yet pinpointing their exact RNA binding sites remains critical for mechanistic understanding and drug optimization. Experimental methods, while precise, are costly and low-throughput, necessitating robust computational alternatives. Approaches based on static feature concatenation may overlook input-dependent relationships between RNA residues and ligand functional groups. Here we present LigRNA, a graph neural network framework that predicts RNA-ligand binding sites through joint cross-modal encoding of both molecules. LigRNA integrates structure-guided language model embeddings with physicochemical features-solvent-accessible surface area and secondary structure types, to construct comprehensive RNA representations. Ligands are encoded as attributed molecular graphs via graph attention networks, preserving atom-level chemical topology rather than compressing molecules into fixed fingerprints. A cross-attention mechanism then enables dynamic, ligand-dependent modulation of RNA nucleotide attention, capturing context-specific interaction patterns. Benchmarked on TE9 and TE18 datasets, LigRNA achieves F1 scores of 0.73 and 0.58, improving on GATRsite by 7.4% and 18.4%, respectively. Ablation studies identify the RNA residual encoder as the most consistent contributor across the two benchmarks. The source code is freely available at https://github.com/WillowWang0216/LigRNA.

last_author.name: Xiong, P.
last_author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Suzhou Institute for Advanced Research

preprints.corresponding_institution: University of Science and Technology of China Suzhou Institute for Advanced Research

preprints.title: MedMCP: An Open Agentic Ecosystem for Medical Imaging Workflows
preprints.abstract: Deep learning has driven rapid progress in medical image analysis, with methods for tasks such as organ segmentation, anomaly detection, and radiology report generation now matching or surpassing expert performance on several benchmarks. While many methods are released as open source, their routine adoption by clinicians and medical researchers remains limited. The bottleneck is not a lack of capable tools, but the absence of infrastructure to make them accessible to non-technical users. To break this barrier, we present MedMCP, an agentic framework that solves this last-mile problem along two axes: (1) a local agentic workspace that lets users apply state-of-the-art image analysis methods through natural language, and (2) a community-driven tool ecosystem that lets developers deploy and distribute capabilities as validated, independently testable servers. MedMCP enforces a strict orchestration-execution boundary in which a local language model translates user intent into workflow plans, while all image analysis is delegated to domain-specific tools. The framework runs entirely on-premise, every side-effecting operation passes through a human-in-the-loop permission gate, and a full provenance trail links each output to the tools, parameters, and inputs that produced it. An inspectable workspace lets users verify intermediate results rather than blindly trusting the agent, and completed sessions distill into deterministic, shareable workflows that re-execute without the agent, turning one-off interactions into reproducible analyses. This paper introduces the project's general idea and describes the design principles that guide its development. Beyond a single toolkit, we envision MedMCP as a community-driven platform where each contributed tool becomes easily accessible, compounding individual efforts into shared capability.

preprints.title: Network-enabled drug repurposing identifies lithium to promote cardiomyocyte proliferation
preprints.abstract: The adult mammalian heart has minimal regenerative capacity, limited in part by endogenous cardiomyocyte (CM) renewal. Although CM proliferation is a promising target in both congenital and adult heart disease, no current therapies specifically target this process. Progress has been hindered by the complexity of CM proliferation signaling networks, which may require systems-level approaches. The overall goal of this study was to leverage systems modeling to identify FDA approved drugs that have the potential to be repurposed towards CM proliferation. To achieve this goal, we developed a computational drug repurposing framework that integrates drug-target interaction data with a previously developed logic-based network model of CM proliferation signaling. Using this framework, we identified 81 drugs that directly target nodes within the CM proliferation network, corresponding to 32 unique drug-target interactions. Virtual screening predicted 5 unique drug-target interactions that increase CM proliferation and 14 that decrease CM proliferation outputs. Lithium, a GSK3{beta} inhibitor widely prescribed for bipolar disorder, was predicted and experimentally validated to promote CM proliferation through a Cyclin D/CDK4 pathway. In vivo, treatment of pregnant mice with lithium increased DNA synthesis in the CMs of their embryos. A retrospective analysis of the FDA Adverse Events Reporting System confirmed that relative to other mood stabilizers, in utero exposure to lithium was associated with an increased incidence of congenital heart defects, in males but not females. Together, this work provides a computational-experimental framework for repurposing FDA-approved drugs to modulate CM proliferation, which highlights therapeutic potential of lithium for adult CM regeneration but congenital risks to developing embryos.

last_author.name: Saucerman, J. J.
last_author.affiliation: University of Virginia

preprints.title: On technical biases in imaging spatial transcriptomics
preprints.abstract: Imaging spatial transcriptomics (iST) has revolutionized our ability to contextualize gene expression within intact tissue architectures at single-cell and subcellular resolution. However, these platforms introduce complex technical biases that span the entire measurement pipeline -- from sample preparation to data acquisition to quantification. Here, we categorize these biases into experimental (e.g., sample preservation and spatial sampling) and computational sources (e.g., z-stack registration and field-of-view stitching). Using public datasets, we demonstrate how different biases can compound and manifest, and propose a unified count modeling framework to formalize these sources of variation. Finally, we call for a more integrated understanding of iST data origins and greater knowledge sharing within and across sectors to support the prospective development of more robust experimental design and reliable downstream analysis.

preprints.title: Order Matters: Ambient RNA correction confounds doublet detection in single-cell RNA sequencing
preprints.abstract: A common technical artifact in droplet-based single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is the capture of two cells in the same droplet, termed doublets. Doublets may present as hybrid cell types, and their removal is a critical step during quality control. Another form of contamination is ambient RNA, which originates from free floating RNA released from other cells in suspension, likely during cell death. As with doublets, ambient RNA results in unexpected gene expression patterns. Most suggested analysis pipelines include ambient RNA correction before doublet detection however no formal investigation into how doublet detection is affected by ambient RNA correction has been conducted. Here, we evaluate the impact of ambient RNA correction on the performance of doublet detection using novel engineered and multiplexed datasets. We apply three of the most widely-used methods for removing ambient RNA (decontX, soupX, CellBender), in conjunction with up to six doublet detection methods (scDblFinder, scds, bcds, cxds, scrublet, DoubletDetection). We find that doublet detection tools perform best when done prior to ambient RNA correction, with the exception of CellBender. Performing ambient RNA correction first, particularly for decontX, leads to an increased proportion of doublet droplets retained in the dataset compared with calling doublets on uncorrected data. We show that both decontX and soupX partially mask doublet signal by removing proportionally more ambient RNA from doublets that remain undetected after ambient RNA correction. Our results show that the performance of doublet detection is significantly impacted by the use of ambient RNA correction tools. We suggest a new workflow that implements doublet detection prior to ambient RNA correction unless using CellBender.

last_author.name: Oshlack, A.
last_author.affiliation: Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre

preprints.title: The lymphangiogenic Ccbe1-Adamts-Vegfc axis shapes cerebrovascular regionalization via selective patterning of fenestrated vascular beds
preprints.abstract: Organ development and function require regional specialization of vascular networks, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a non-canonical role for the lymphangiogenic Ccbe1-Adamts-Vegfc axis in shaping cerebrovascular regionalization in zebrafish. A ccbe1 knock-in reporter revealed highly restricted expression in the developing brain, with its genetic loss causing early vascularization defects at the pineal gland-choroid plexus interface. Simultaneous Vegfa signaling deficiency markedly exacerbated these regional vascular defects, accompanied by disrupted blood flow, local hemorrhage, and choroid plexus epithelial disorganization, while largely preserving neighboring barrier-forming vessels. Loss of vegfc closely phenocopied ccbe1 mutant defects, with fenestrated vascular patterning requiring both Vegfr2 and Vegfr3 signaling, whereas disruption of adamts3 and adamts14 indicated region-specific requirements for Vegfc-activating proteases. Conversely, pineal gland-specific overexpression of activated Vegfc partially rescued the vascularization defects. Collectively, these findings suggest that spatially restricted Ccbe1-Adamts-Vegfc activity provides angiogenic signaling specificity enabling fenestrated cerebrovascular patterning and regionalization.

last_author.name: Matsuoka, R. L.
last_author.affiliation: Department of Neurosciences, Cleveland Clinic Research, Cleveland, USA

preprints.title: TiSAM: fusing spatial and histopathology foundation models for whole-slide image segmentation
preprints.abstract: Semantic segmentation of whole-slide images (WSIs) quantifies tissue composition and architecture, but existing models require extensive annotation and lose accuracy as the number of tissue classes increases or on heterogeneous, cross-scanner datasets. Here, we present the Tissue Segment Anything Model (TiSAM), which fuses SAM3 spatial features with UNI2-h pathology features within a multi-scale decoder. Because public benchmarks contain few tissue classes, we release MegaMouse, comprising 36,833 annotations of 52 tissue classes from 12 mouse organs, and an 11-class human pancreas dataset. TiSAM achieved the highest overall performance across four public datasets compared to existing convolutional neural network and vision transformer models, maintained high accuracy on MegaMouse, and maintained high accuracy in the human pancreas dataset when trained on as few as 5 annotated WSIs where previous integrations of SAM with pathology foundation models did not. TiSAM segmentations were also more consistent across eight slide scanners compared to other models. These results establish TiSAM as a general and highly adaptable framework for tissue segmentation, enabling studies containing many tissue classes, limited annotations, or images from multiple scanners.

last_author.name: Kiemen, A. L.
last_author.affiliation: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine

preprints.title: A Quarter-Power Law for Translating Human Development intoEquivalent Mouse and Rat Ages
preprints.abstract: Translating developmental time between laboratory rodents and humans is a central problem in preclinical research, yet no consensus mathematical framework exists. Linear models are known to be inadequate, and the logarithmic transformations conventionally used in the field do not fully linearize the relationship. Here we evaluated seven candidate functional forms relating human developmental age to rodent age, using a curated dataset of homologous developmental milestones in mouse, rat and human. Models were fitted by weighted nonlinear least squares and compared by leave-one-out cross-validation under a single model-independent weighting scheme derived from a LOESS variance estimate. Model specification was assessed using heteroscedasticity-robust RESET tests, which revealed significant residual curvature for the raw, logarithmic and log--log transformations, whereas the quarter-power transformation (X = Human1/4) was the only one leaving no detectable curvature in either species (mouse F = 0.90, p = 0.407; rat F = 1.83, p = 0.163). A quarter-power model with an additive constant (y = bx1/4 + c) achieved the lowest cross-validated error in mice and performed nearly as well as the best-performing model in rats, a free-power model with an additive constant, while using one fewer parameter. A third-power formulation, evaluated in light of the ongoing debate over metabolic scaling exponents, never ranked first in either species. Joint models incorporating a species dummy variable further supported a common quarter-power structure across both species, with species-specific coefficients. The additive constant was required in every formulation, indicating a systematic offset between developmental timescales that a purely scale-invariant power law does not capture. The resulting model provides a parsimonious, empirically supported framework for estimating equivalent developmental ages across humans, mice and rats.

last_author.name: Vazquez, P.
last_author.affiliation: CONICET

preprints.title: A genomic foundation model for interpreting human genetic diversity
preprints.abstract: Interpreting human genomes requires models that recognize shared biological functions while accounting for variation underlying traits, disease susceptibility and adaptation. Here we present hEVO, a genomic foundation model trained on 4.784 billion distinct haplotype sequences reconstructed from whole genome sequencing (WGS) data for 63,809 individuals selected from 550,237 samples across eight cohorts. Pretraining integrates shared sequence features and naturally occurring allelic differences without clinical or functional labels. Against representatives of the Evo 2, NT, GPN and other genomic model families, hEVO ranked first in 18 of 19 primary comparisons spanning functional annotation, variant interpretation and human evolution. Its pretrained allele scores generalized across all six complementary variant benchmarks without task-specific training, achieving the highest performance across clinical pathogenicity, fine-mapped causal variants and experimentally measured regulatory effects. Retrospective ClinVar reclassification further demonstrated improved identification of pathogenic classifications later downgraded, supporting reassessment of earlier clinical interpretations. Predictive strengths extended to ancestry inference, human accelerated sequences and preference for reported selected alleles. This breadth was achieved with substantially fewer parameters than billion-parameter comparators and low inference overhead in the evaluated workloads. These findings establish human haplotype diversity as a source of transferable biological information for interpreting both the disruption of genome function and the variation retained during human evolution.

last_author.name: Li, M. J.
last_author.affiliation: Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center, Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou, China; Department of Bioinformatics, The Province and Ministry Co-sponso
